Sumimi v0.4.5 — **the second engine becomes a witness: it caught three real
bugs, and the engine's limit gets its third bill**.

**One fix, and it was not cosmetic.** The SQLite backend stored timestamps in
**seconds** while DuckDB stores **microseconds**. Three user-visible bugs came
from that one difference:

| # | the difference | what a user saw | the fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | the API's precision | DuckDB's `visitDuration` had a decimal, SQLite's did not | both are microseconds now (schema v7) |
| 2 | the window's edge | an event in the **last second** of a range counted on one engine only | the same window on both |
| 3 | the duration | `visit_duration` was 1 000× too large | the µs difference, divided by 1 000 000 |

The SQLite databases migrate themselves: **schema v7** multiplies the stored
timestamps by a million.

**The second engine is now a correctness oracle.** `service/tests/backends_agree.rs`
writes **the same events into both engines** and compares **every report, row by
row, in the same order** — the summary, all thirteen dimensions, the timeseries,
the custom events, the query strings, the sessions, the event log. A difference
is a bug, whichever engine is wrong. It found the three above on its first run.

**And the measurements became routine.** The engine comparison is now a CI job
on every push, and the tool that makes it is public (`sumimi-gotest`) — a second
implementation, so the measurement does not inherit the server's bugs.

**The two engines, on the same three-year history** (6 227 088 page views):

| | **DuckDB** | **SQLite** |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| the peak memory under load (20 000/s) | 214 MB | **33 MB** |
| the data on disk (three years) | **372 MB** | 3 086 MB |
| the summary of the last year | **145 ms** | 17 452 ms |
| the summary of the last three years | **186 ms** | 24 162 ms |

![The report over a range](https://x-cmd.com/draw?h=520&labels=6+months%2C1+year%2C3+years&series=DuckDB+%28ms%29%3A94%2C193%2C206&series=SQLite+%28ms%29%3A13522%2C28824%2C23509&line=how+many+times+slower%3A144%2C149%2C114&title=The+report+over+a+range&type=combo&w=960)

DuckDB wins the disk (8×) and the latency (95–238×) and **loses the memory**
(6.6×). That is the trade, and it is not "DuckDB is better".

**The engine's limit has a third bill: disk.** The limit does not decide
whether a report can be answered — DuckDB **spills to disk** and answers
anyway. What it decides is how fast, and how much disk it costs on the way.
The same three-year history, the same report, four limits:

| the engine's limit | the report | the peak memory | the spill on disk |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 512 MB | **133 ms** | 571 MB | 0 |
| 256 MB | 187 ms | 344 MB | 27 MB |
| 128 MB | 384 ms | 225 MB | 97 MB |
| 64 MB | 734 ms | **154 MB** | 140 MB |

![The limit trades memory for time and disk](https://x-cmd.com/draw?h=520&labels=512MB%2C256MB%2C128MB%2C64MB&line=the+report+%28s%29%3A0.133%2C0.187%2C0.384%2C0.734&series=the+peak+memory+%28MB%29%3A571.3%2C344.6%2C225.3%2C154.4&series=the+spill+on+disk+%28MB%29%3A0%2C27.3%2C97.8%2C140.6&title=The+limit+trades+memory+for+time+and+disk&type=combo&w=960)

**The answer is the same at every limit** — the same page views, the same
visitors, the same bounces, byte for byte. So the limit is a **trade**: memory
for time and disk. At 64 MB the report is 5.5× slower and it needs 140 MB of
temporary disk to do it.

Two things follow, and one of them corrects what we said before:

* **the process runs 60–97 MB above the engine's limit** (the code, the
  allocator's arenas and the query's own vectors are not the buffer manager's
  business) — so the rule for sizing a box is still **the engine's
  `memory_limit` plus about 60 MB**, and not more than the tier;
* **the spill is a peak, not growth** — DuckDB deletes it when the query ends —
  but it is disk, and the server's own ceiling on it is
  `max_temp_directory_size`: **2 GB by default**
  (`SUMIMI_DUCKDB_TEMP_LIMIT`). On a 10 GB VPS that is a fifth of the disk in
  one query, and **a spill that cannot fit is a failed report, not a slow one**.
  Set the ceiling to what the disk can spare.

The deployment documentation now says all of this, with the same charts.

**Also in this release**

* the report charts are **links** — the data lives in the URL, so a chart can
  be pasted into an issue, a release note or a repository and it renders there
  with nothing installed;
* the CI has a **routine job** for the four axes, and the load generator's
  version is pinned, so the published numbers do not move under the reader's
  feet;
* the heartbeat's memory is the **sum** over DuckDB's tags (that was v0.4.4).
